title: National Nutritional Foods Association v. Weinberger
lead: The Food and Drug Administration uses notice and comment to make concentrated vitamin A and D preparations prescription drugs. The manufacturers’ challenge separates the agency’s power to make binding rules from its missing explanation of why these products qualify as drugs.

actors.name: National Nutritional Foods Association and Solgar
actors.role: Trade association and manufacturer challenging vitamin regulations.

actors.name: Food and Drug Administration Commissioner
actors.role: Agency official adopting the classifications and prescription restrictions.

actors.name: Judge Frankel
actors.role: District judge granting the government summary judgment.

proceedings: Preliminary relief was denied and that denial affirmed; a separate direct-review petition was dismissed for want of jurisdiction.
The district court later granted summary judgment for the government and vacated a deposition notice.
The Second Circuit remanded for examination of the full administrative record and an adequate explanation, without immediately invalidating the rules.
limits: This transforms the canonical 1975 brief without a fresh audit or certification of current vitamin regulation, earlier companion proceedings, or later remand outcomes. The prescription-status discussion was conditional on rational antecedent drug classification. Lumbard’s concurrence did not replace the majority’s statutory review standard.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The Commissioner proposes restrictions based on toxicity and therapeutic promotion
sections.cue: What doses and participation process were involved?
paragraphs: The Food and Drug Administration proposed treating vitamin A above 10,000 international units per dosage form and vitamin D above 400 international units as prescription drugs. The December 14, 1972 proposal invoked § 701(a) of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, a general grant for efficient-enforcement regulations.

It described prolonged excessive intake causing toxicity and sometimes death, widespread disease-prevention and treatment promotion, and recommended nutritional allowances much lower for most people. The Commissioner made a medical bibliography available and allowed sixty days of comments.

More than 2,500 submissions came from consumers, clinicians, manufacturers, associations, and others. Some favored restrictions, some accepted toxicity but urged higher thresholds, and some viewed vitamins as foods subject to consumer choice. National Nutritional Foods Association and Solgar submitted extensive objections.

sections.title: Final rules take effect while the challengers seek judicial relief
paragraphs: On August 2, 1973, the Commissioner announced rules effective October 1. He reasoned that existing nutritional ranges met ordinary needs and higher amounts ordinarily served therapy. A recognized exception allowed vitamin D up to 1,000 international units under medical supervision for poor absorption.

The association and Solgar sued August 6. Judge Frankel denied preliminary relief, and the Second Circuit affirmed that earlier decision. After effectiveness, Frankel granted summary judgment dismissing the complaint on April 5, 1974. He accepted notice and comment, applied arbitrary-and-capricious review rather than a new trial, and vacated a notice to depose the Commissioner. A separate direct appellate petition had been dismissed for lack of jurisdiction. This appeal concerned final summary judgment.

sections.title: The majority upholds authority to make binding rules under the general grant
sections.cue: Why were formal-hearing provisions not exclusive?
paragraphs: The challengers argued that only § 701(e) rules, adopted through specified objections, requested evidentiary hearings, and appellate review, could bind private parties. Section 701(a), they said, supplied interpretations for courts to consider independently in enforcement suits.

Judge Mansfield, joined by Judge Waterman, rejected that rigid distinction despite textual uncertainty about authoritative effect. General delegations could permit substantive rules, especially where scientific expertise and industry-wide analysis improved on repeated case-by-case litigation. The Supreme Court’s Hynson, Ciba, Bentex, and USV decisions recognized administrative new-drug determinations, evidentiary standards, and rejection of deficient applications without futile hearings, not parallel systems requiring a fresh judicial decision for every producer.

The special hearing scheme supplemented rather than exhausted the general grant. Binding informal rules still required Administrative Procedure Act notice and comment; calling them interpretive could not evade that duty. The majority also rejected a claim that the Durham-Humphrey prescription-drug amendment withheld rulemaking power. Conflicting history gave greater weight to the final Senate report than earlier individual statements, and recognized authority over new-drug status supported prescription classifications too.

sections.title: Written participation is sufficient, but review still requires an explanation
sections.cue: Why was a new scientific trial not the remedy?
paragraphs: About forty-six folders contained comments, medical material, and detailed critiques. The issue was appraisal of scientific risks, not credibility or a narrow historical fact, so trial-type hearings were unnecessary. The Commissioner acknowledged that consumers could swallow many weak tablets but thought convenient concentrated doses increased excess-consumption risk.

Administrative Procedure Act § 706(2)(A)’s arbitrary-and-capricious standard governed informal rulemaking, not § 706(2)(E)’s substantial-evidence standard for the distinguished hearing proceedings. Still, a concise basis-and-purpose statement had to permit meaningful review; unexplained action could not survive just because no formal hearing record existed. Agency experience used as evidence belonged in the reviewable record.

Camp and Overton Park, precedents governing judicial examination of agency reasoning, kept focus on material before the agency. Explanatory affidavits or testimony could clarify reasoning, but inadequate explanation did not license an independent merits trial. If the finding lacked support in that record, the appropriate response was vacatur and remand rather than judicial scientific substitution.

sections.title: The agency has not adequately explained the antecedent drug classification
sections.cue: Why did toxicity alone leave a missing step?
paragraphs: Section 201(g) included articles intended to diagnose, cure, mitigate, treat, or prevent disease. Lack of nutritional usefulness at higher doses did not alone establish that intent. In a separate 1974 National Nutritional Foods Association v. FDA case, the circuit had invalidated a broader above-recommended-allowance rule. Pharmacopoeia listing offered afterward was not the agency’s actual reason, and nutritional uselessness did not establish therapy.

That precedent did not automatically decide this dispute. Here vitamin A’s threshold exceeded 10,000 rather than 8,000 international units, a vitamin D exception accommodated nutrition, only two vitamins were regulated, and the review framework differed. Therapeutic promotion, labels, or almost exclusively therapeutic use might establish objective intent. But incomplete final reasoning and an incomplete supplied record prevented the court from assuming that potentially sufficient explanation was the agency’s actual supported basis.

sections.title: Prescription status is defensible if drug status is rationally established
sections.cue: What inquiry was ordered on remand?
paragraphs: If these preparations qualified as drugs, § 503(b)(1)(B) allowed assessment of toxicity, harmful effects, use methods, and needed precautions. The challengers conceded toxicity at sufficient levels. Routine concentrated intake could be dangerous despite theoretically safe use. Foods and aspirin did not show irrational disparate treatment on this consumption record, and food-derived vitamins could increase tablet risks. Decholin differed because toxicity was unproved and practical use safe.

The court remanded for an Overton Park-type inquiry into the entire administrative record, with explanatory affidavits or testimony as needed. If drug classification was rational, the regulations could be upheld and summary judgment stand; if irrational, summary judgment had to be vacated. It neither found therapeutic intent itself, immediately struck the rules, nor granted a de novo trial.

sections.title: Lumbard stresses close review as substantive rulemaking expands
sections.cue: What did the unanimous remand leave undecided?
paragraphs: Judge Lumbard concurred. He was less certain of Congress’s original prescription-rulemaking intent, but statutory breadth, no clear contrary history, and later judicial developments persuaded him the Supreme Court would recognize the authority.

He urged serious examination of evidence rather than approval of anything short of total irrationality as courts expanded substantive power under old general grants. In substance, unsupported rules could abuse discretion for lack of substantial evidentiary support. He thought Frankel’s actual review approached that standard, but joined the need for fuller explanation. That was his understanding of meaningful review, not adoption of § 706(2)(E) by the majority.
All three judges agreed on remand on February 3, 1975. Binding-rule authority survived the challenge; the particular drug-classification foundation remained to be examined.
